claim: Dynein-2 is the retrograde motor for intraflagellar transport.
source: The dynein-2 microtubule motor is the retrograde motor for intraflagellar transport.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about dynein-2 function.

claim: Mutations in dynein-2 components cause skeletal ciliopathies, notably Jeune syndrome.
source: Mutations in dynein-2 components cause skeletal ciliopathies, notably Jeune syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dynein-2 contains a heterodimer of two non-identical intermediate chains, WDR34 and WDR60.
source: Dynein-2 contains a heterodimer of two non-identical intermediate chains, WDR34 and WDR60.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a structural feature of dynein-2.

claim: WDR34 KO cells can assemble a dynein-2 motor complex that binds IFT proteins.
source: Using quantitative proteomics, we show that WDR34 KO cells can assemble a dynein-2 motor complex that binds IFT proteins yet fails to extend an axoneme, indicating complex function is stalled.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative proteomics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: WDR34 KO cells fail to extend an axoneme.
source: Using quantitative proteomics, we show that WDR34 KO cells can assemble a dynein-2 motor complex that binds IFT proteins yet fails to extend an axoneme, indicating complex function is stalled.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data showing lack of axoneme extension.

claim: WDR60 KO cells extend axonemes.
source: In contrast, WDR60 KO cells do extend axonemes but show reduced assembly of dynein-2 and binding to IFT proteins.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy data.

claim: WDR60 KO cells show reduced assembly of dynein-2 and binding to IFT proteins.
source: In contrast, WDR60 KO cells do extend axonemes but show reduced assembly of dynein-2 and binding to IFT proteins.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic analysis showing reduced interactions.

claim: Both WDR34 and WDR60 are required to maintain a functional transition zone.
source: Both proteins are required to maintain a functional transition zone and for efficient bidirectional intraflagellar transport.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered localization of transition zone markers.

claim: Both WDR34 and WDR60 are required for efficient bidirectional intraflagellar transport.
source: Both proteins are required to maintain a functional transition zone and for efficient bidirectional intraflagellar transport.
evidence: This is supported by data showing accumulation of IFT proteins in knockout cells.

claim: The subunit asymmetry within the dynein-2 complex is matched with a functional asymmetry between the dynein-2 intermediate chains.
source: Our results indicate that the subunit asymmetry within the dynein-2 complex is matched with a functional asymmetry between the dynein-2 intermediate chains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential phenotypes observed in WDR34 vs WDR60 KO cells.

claim: Loss of function of dynein-2 leads to defects in transition zone architecture.
source: Furthermore, this work reveals that loss of function of dynein-2 leads to defects in transition zone architecture, as well as intraflagellar transport.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered localization of transition zone markers RPGRIP1L and TMEM67.

claim: Dynein-1 is involved in the transport of cargos in the cytoplasm, organelle dynamics and in mitotic spindle organization during mitosis.
source: The better-characterized dynein-1 is involved in the transport of cargos in the cytoplasm, organelle dynamics and in mitotic spindle organization during mitosis (Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts et al., 2013.

claim: Dynein-2 is responsible for retrograde transport in cilia and flagella.
source: Dynein-2 is responsible for retrograde transport in cilia and flagella.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dynein-2 function.

claim: Primary cilia are hair-like extensions present on almost all animal cells that act as antennae for extracellular signals.
source: Primary (non-motile) cilia are hair-like extensions present on almost all animal cells that act as antennae for extracellular signals and are fundamental to proper metazoan development and ongoing health.
evidence: This is established knowledge about primary cilia.

claim: Primary cilia integrate signals in key pathways including sonic hedgehog (Shh), Wnt and platelet-derived growth factor signaling.
source: They integrate signals in key pathways including sonic hedgehog (Shh), Wnt and platelet-derived growth factor signaling and participate in metabolic control and autophagy (Reiter and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Reiter and Leroux, 2017.

claim: Cilia are particularly important to ensure correct Shh signaling during embryonic development.
source: Cilia are particularly important to ensure correct Shh signaling during embryonic development (Goetz and Anderson, 2010; He et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goetz and Anderson, 2010 and He et al., 2017.

claim: Defects in cilia are linked to many human diseases, known collectively as ciliopathies.
source: Defects in cilia are linked to many human diseases, known collectively as ciliopathies, including developmental disorders, neurodegeneration and metabolic diseases (Reiter and Leroux, 2017; Yee and Reiter, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reiter and Leroux, 2017 and Yee and Reiter, 2015.

claim: Ciliogenesis is initiated in non-dividing cells by the docking of pre-ciliary vesicles with the mother centriole.
source: Ciliogenesis is initiated in non-dividing cells by the docking of pre-ciliary vesicles with the mother centriole.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliogenesis.

claim: A transition zone separates the mother centriole from the main length of the axoneme and forms a diffusion barrier for both soluble and membrane proteins at the base of the cilium.
source: A 'transition zone' (TZ) that separates the mother centriole from the main length of the axoneme forms a diffusion barrier for both soluble and membrane proteins at the base of the cilium (Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2011; Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garcia-Gonzalo et al., 2011 and Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2017.

claim: IFT-B complexes undergo kinesin-2-driven motility from base to tip.
source: IFT-B complexes (comprising of a core subcomplex of nine subunits (IFT88, −81, –74, −70, –52, −46, –27, −25, and −22) with five additional, peripherally-associated subunits (IFT172, −80, –57, −54, and −20)) undergo kinesin-2-driven motility from base to tip where the complexes are then reorganized prior to retrograde transport of IFT-A (comprising six subunits (IFT144, -140, -139, -122, -121/WDR35, and -43)) driven by dynein-2 (Hou and Witman, 2015; Jensen and Leroux, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hou and Witman, 2015 and Jensen and Leroux, 2017.

claim: Dynein-2 is built around a heavy chain dimer of DHC2/DYNC2H1.
source: Dynein-2 is built around a heavy chain dimer of DHC2/DYNC2H1 (Criswell et al., 1996; Mikami et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Criswell et al., 1996 and Mikami et al., 2002.

claim: WDR34 and WDR60 were first identified as dynein-2 subunits named FAP133 and FAP163 in Chlamydomonas.
source: This associates with two intermediate chains (ICs), WDR34 and WDR60, first identified as dynein-2 subunits named FAP133 and FAP163 in Chlamydomonas (Patel-King et al., 2013; Rompolas et al., 2007) and subsequently shown to be components of metazoan dynein-2 (Asante et al., 2013; Asante et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patel-King et al., 2013 and Rompolas et al., 2007.

claim: The asymmetry of dynein-2 intermediate chains distinguishes dynein-2 from dynein-1 where two identical IC subunits form the holoenzyme.
source: This asymmetry distinguishes dynein-2 from dynein-1 where two identical IC subunits form the holoenzyme.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between dynein-1 and dynein-2.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding dynein-2 subunits are associated with skeletal ciliopathies, notably short rib-polydactyly syndromes (SRPSs) and Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (JATD, Jeune syndrome).
source: Mutations in genes encoding dynein-2 subunits are associated with skeletal ciliopathies, notably short rib-polydactyly syndromes (SRPSs) and Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (JATD, Jeune syndrome).
evidence: This is established knowledge about disease associations.

claim: A range of mutations affecting DYNC2H1 have been identified in skeletal ciliopathies.
source: In recent years, whole exome-sequencing technology has enabled the identification of new mutations involved in skeletal ciliopathies, notably a range of mutations affecting DYNC2H1 (DHC2, [Chen et al., 2016; Cossu et al., 2016; Dagoneau et al., 2009; El Hokayem et al., 2012; Mei et al., 2015; Merrill et al., 2009; Okamoto et al., 2015; Schmidts et al., 2013a]).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying DYNC2H1 mutations.

claim: Mutations in WDR34 have been reported in skeletal ciliopathies.
source: Additionally, mutations in WDR34 (Huber et al., 2013; Schmidts et al., 2013b), WDR60 (Cossu et al., 2016; McInerney-Leo et al., 2013), LIC3/DYNC2LI1 (Kessler et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2015) and TCTEX1D2 (Schmidts et al., 2015) have also been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huber et al., 2013 and Schmidts et al., 2013b.

claim: Mutations in WDR60 have been reported in skeletal ciliopathies.
source: Additionally, mutations in WDR34 (Huber et al., 2013; Schmidts et al., 2013b), WDR60 (Cossu et al., 2016; McInerney-Leo et al., 2013), LIC3/DYNC2LI1 (Kessler et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2015) and TCTEX1D2 (Schmidts et al., 2015) have also been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cossu et al., 2016 and McInerney-Leo et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of dynein heavy chain results in short, stumpy cilia that accumulate IFT particles at the tip.
source: In all cases, loss of dynein heavy chain results in short, stumpy cilia that accumulate IFT particles at the tip, consistent with the role of dynein-2 in retrograde ciliary transport (Hou and Witman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hou and Witman, 2015.

claim: LIC3/DYNC2LI1 plays an important role in ciliogenesis and stabilization of the entire dynein-2 complex.
source: Two studies in Chlamydomonas and in human patient-derived fibroblasts revealed that LIC3/DYNC2LI1 (D1bLIC in Chlamydomonas) plays an important role in ciliogenesis and stabilization of the entire dynein-2 complex (Li et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2015 and Taylor et al., 2015.

claim: Loss of Tctex2b (TCTEX1D2) destabilizes dynein-2 and reduces IFT in Chlamydomonas.
source: Similarly, loss of Tctex2b (TCTEX1D2) destabilizes dynein-2 and reduces IFT in Chlamydomonas (Schmidts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schmidts et al., 2015.

claim: Knockdown of WDR60 or WDR34 in hTERT-RPE1 cells results in a reduction of ciliated cells.
source: Knockdown of WDR60 or WDR34 in hTERT-RPE1 cells results in a reduction of ciliated cells, with an increase in length of the remaining cilia, likely depending on depletion efficiency (Asante et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Asante et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations in WDR34 result in short cilia with a bulbous ciliary tip in patient fibroblast cells affected by SRP.
source: Mutations in WDR34 have also been shown to result in short cilia with a bulbous ciliary tip in patient fibroblast cells affected by SRP (Huber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huber et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of WDR34 in mice results in short and stumpy cilia with an abnormal accumulation of ciliary proteins and defects in Shh signaling.
source: Consistent with the results obtained in patient cells, loss of WDR34 in mice also results in short and stumpy cilia with an abnormal accumulation of ciliary proteins and defects in Shh signaling (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations in WDR60 patient fibroblasts are associated with a reduction in cilia number.
source: Similarly, mutations in WDR60 patient fibroblasts are associated with a reduction in cilia number, although the percentage of ciliated cells was variable in different affected individuals (McInerney-Leo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McInerney-Leo et al., 2013.

claim: WDR60 plays a major role in retrograde ciliary protein trafficking.
source: Moreover, further recent data found that WDR60 plays a major role in retrograde ciliary protein trafficking (Hamada et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: Two WDR34 KO clones were derived using guide RNAs targeting exons 2 and 3.
source: We derived two WDR34 KO clones (1 and 2) using guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting exons 2 and 3, and one KO clone for WDR60, targeting exon 3.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used to generate knockout cell lines.

claim: One WDR60 KO clone was derived targeting exon 3.
source: We derived two WDR34 KO clones (1 and 2) using guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting exons 2 and 3, and one KO clone for WDR60, targeting exon 3.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used to generate knockout cell lines.

claim: Neither WDR34 nor WDR60 was detected in the respective KO cells compared to the controls.
source: Neither WDR34 nor WDR60 was detected in the respective KO cells compared to the controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Defects in ciliogenesis in both WDR34 and WDR60 KO cells were rescued by overexpressing WT proteins.
source: Defects in ciliogenesis in both WDR34 and WDR60 KO cells were rescued by overexpressing WT proteins, confirming that the phenotypes we observed were not due to off-target mutations (described below).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of WDR34 severely impaired the ability of the KO cells to extend a microtubule axoneme.
source: Loss of WDR34 severely impaired the ability of the KO cells to extend a microtubule axoneme (Figure 1A,B), although Arl13b localized within those few cilia that did form.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Arl13b localized within those few cilia that did form in WDR34 KO cells.
source: Loss of WDR34 severely impaired the ability of the KO cells to extend a microtubule axoneme (Figure 1A,B), although Arl13b localized within those few cilia that did form.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Loss of WDR60 did not significantly affect the ability of cells to extend an axoneme.
source: In contrast, loss of WDR60 did not significantly affect the ability of cells to extend an axoneme (Figure 1B) but did result in a change in localization of Arl13b to a more pronounced enrichment at the base and tip of many cilia compared to the more uniform ciliary distribution in control cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Loss of WDR60 resulted in a change in localization of Arl13b to a more pronounced enrichment at the base and tip of many cilia.
source: In contrast, loss of WDR60 did not significantly affect the ability of cells to extend an axoneme (Figure 1B) but did result in a change in localization of Arl13b to a more pronounced enrichment at the base and tip of many cilia compared to the more uniform ciliary distribution in control cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cilia were shorter in both WDR60 and WDR34 KO cells.
source: Cilia were shorter in both WDR60 and WDR34 KO cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cilium length shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WDR34 KO cells failed to extend an axoneme.
source: In contrast, WDR34 KO cells failed to extend an axoneme (Figure 1E) but showed a large docked pre-ciliary vesicle, consistent with the small Arl13b-positive structures seen by immunofluorescence.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: WDR34 KO cells showed a large docked pre-ciliary vesicle.
source: In contrast, WDR34 KO cells failed to extend an axoneme (Figure 1E) but showed a large docked pre-ciliary vesicle, consistent with the small Arl13b-positive structures seen by immunofluorescence.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: WDR60 KO cells showed apparently normal cilia with normal basal body structures and axoneme extension.
source: WDR60 KO cells showed apparently normal cilia (Figure 1F) with normal basal body structures and axoneme extension.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: WDR60 KO cells showed a bulged cilium tip containing accumulated electron dense particles.
source: However, when an entire cilium was captured in WDR60 KO serial sections (Figure 1G), we observed a bulged cilium tip containing accumulated electron dense particles (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: The ciliary membrane bulged at a second point along the axoneme in WDR60 KO cells and this region contained intraciliary vesicular structures.
source: To our surprise, we also observed the ciliary membrane bulged at a second point along the axoneme and this region contained intraciliary vesicular structures (Figure 1Hi).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1Hi.

claim: IFT88 was found almost exclusively at the base of the cilia in WT RPE1 cells after 24 hr serum starvation.
source: After 24 hr serum starvation, IFT88 (part of IFT-B) was found almost exclusively at the base of the cilia in WT RPE1 cells but in WDR60 KO and WDR34 KO cells IFT88 was found throughout the cilia and accumulated at the tips (Figure 2A and B, quantified in Figure 1Ai).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: In WDR60 KO and WDR34 KO cells IFT88 was found throughout the cilia and accumulated at the tips.
source: After 24 hr serum starvation, IFT88 (part of IFT-B) was found almost exclusively at the base of the cilia in WT RPE1 cells but in WDR60 KO and WDR34 KO cells IFT88 was found throughout the cilia and accumulated at the tips (Figure 2A and B, quantified in Figure 1Ai).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: IFT-B proteins were seen to accumulate at the tip of cilia in WDR34 KO cells that did extend cilia.
source: In those WDR34 KO cells that did extend cilia, IFT-B proteins were seen to accumulate at the tip of cilia.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data for IFT-B proteins.

claim: IFT20 was enriched at both the tip and the base of cilia in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Another IFT-B protein, IFT20 (Figure 2E), was enriched at both the tip and the base of cilia in WDR60 KO cells (quantification in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and quantification in Figure 2F.

claim: IFT20 is the only IFT component found to localize to the Golgi.
source: IFT20 is the only IFT component found to localize to the Golgi until now.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about IFT20.

claim: The Golgi pool of IFT20-GFP was largely absent from WDR60 KO cells.
source: This pool of IFT20-GFP was largely absent from WDR60 KO cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both IFT140 and IFT43 were accumulated along the length of the axoneme within cilia in WDR60 KO cells.
source: We found that both IFT140 (Figure 3A) and IFT43 (Figure 3B) were accumulated along the length of the axoneme within cilia in WDR60 KO cells, as well as at the tips in the few cilia present in WDR34 KO cells, while they were found only at the base of the cilia in WT cells (quantification in Figure 3Ai–iii and 3Bi-iii).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: IFT140 and IFT43 accumulated at the tips in the few cilia present in WDR34 KO cells.
source: We found that both IFT140 (Figure 3A) and IFT43 (Figure 3B) were accumulated along the length of the axoneme within cilia in WDR60 KO cells, as well as at the tips in the few cilia present in WDR34 KO cells, while they were found only at the base of the cilia in WT cells (quantification in Figure 3Ai–iii and 3Bi-iii).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Both IFT140 and IFT43 are enriched in WDR60 KO cilia compared to controls.
source: Further quantification showed that both IFT140 (Figure 3C) and IFT43 (Figure 3D) are enriched in WDR60 KO cilia compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: KAP3 accumulated at the ciliary tip in WDR60 KO cells.
source: In addition, we determined the localization of a subunit of the anterograde kinesin-2 motor, KAP3 which was also accumulated at the ciliary tip in WDR60 KO cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Arl13b-GFP and EGFP-SSTR3 localize at the ciliary tip in WDR60 KO cells.
source: We found that in live cells Arl13b-GFP and EGFP-SSTR3 localize at the ciliary tip in WDR60 KO cells, which appear enlarged and bulbous in these cells, consistent with EM data (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: There is a consistent reduction in the amount of Arl13b-GFP within cilia in WDR60 KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: We also noticed a consistent reduction in the amount of Arl13b-GFP within cilia in WDR60 KO cells compared to WT cells (Figure 4C and Ci).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4C and Ci.

claim: EGFP-SSTR3 is reduced in WDR60 KO cilia compared to WT cells.
source: The same observation was made with EGFP-SSTR3 (Figure 4D and Di) and EGFP-5HT6 (Figure 4E and Ei).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D and Di.

claim: EGFP-5HT6 is reduced in WDR60 KO cilia compared to WT cells.
source: The same observation was made with EGFP-SSTR3 (Figure 4D and Di) and EGFP-5HT6 (Figure 4E and Ei).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4E and Ei.

claim: GFP-Rab8a localization in the cilia was indistinguishable between WT and WDR60 KO cells.
source: In contrast, GFP-Rab8a localization in the cilia was indistinguishable between WT and WDR60 KO cells (Figure 4F and Fi).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4F and Fi.

claim: RPGRIP1L is no longer restricted to an area adjacent to the mother centriole in WDR60 KO cells.
source: We found that the core transition zone marker, RPGRIP1L (also known as MKS5), is no longer restricted to an area adjacent to the mother centriole in WDR60 KO cells (Figure 5A, quantified in 5Ai).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and quantification in 5Ai.

claim: TMEM67 becomes much more tightly restricted to the base of the cilium in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Conversely, TMEM67 (also known as MKS3), which in WT cilia extends from the basal body through a more distal region, becomes much more tightly restricted to the base of the cilium in WDR60 KO cells (Figure 5B, quantified in 5Bi).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B and quantification in 5Bi.

claim: The few cilia found in the WDR34 KO cells recapitulate the same phenotype observed in the WDR60 KO cilia with an expansion of RPGRIP1L to a more distal position and a reduction of the TMEM67 domain.
source: The few cilia found in the WDR34 KO cells recapitulate the same phenotype observed in the WDR60 KO cilia with an expansion of RPGRIP1L to a more distal position and a reduction of the TMEM67 domain (Figure 5A and Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: No changes were observed for the transition zone marker TCTN1 in both WDR34 KO and WDR60 KO cells with respect to the control.
source: In contrast to TMEM67 and RPGRIP1L, no changes were observed for the transition zone marker TCTN1 in both WDR34 KO and WDR60 KO cells with respect to the control (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Smo was localized to cilia in WDR60 KO cells even in the absence of SAG stimulation.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that Smo was localized to cilia in WDR60 KO cells even in the absence of SAG stimulation (Figure 6A and Ai).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and Ai.

claim: Smo localization in WDR60 KO cells did not increase upon SAG treatment.
source: This localization did not increase upon agonist treatment.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data comparing SAG-treated and untreated WDR60 KO cells.

claim: Smo was excluded from cilia in WT cells at steady state.
source: In contrast, Smo was indeed excluded from cilia in WT cells at steady state (Figure 6A and Ai) but was readily detected within cilia following SAG stimulation (Figure 6B, Bi, and Bii).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and Ai.

claim: Smo was readily detected within cilia in WT cells following SAG stimulation.
source: In contrast, Smo was indeed excluded from cilia in WT cells at steady state (Figure 6A and Ai) but was readily detected within cilia following SAG stimulation (Figure 6B, Bi, and Bii).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B, Bi, and Bii.

claim: Expression of WT HA-WDR60 and HA-WDR60[T749M] efficiently rescued defects in the localization of IFT88.
source: Both WT HA-WDR60 and HA-WDR60[T749M] efficiently rescued defects in the localization of IFT88 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Expression of HA-WDR60[Q631*] was unable to restore the basal body localization of IFT88.
source: However, expression of HA-WDR60[Q631*] was unable to restore the basal body localization of IFT88 (Figure 7B and Bi).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Bi.

claim: Expression of both WT and the HA-WDR60[T749M] mutant of WDR60 restored the localization of IFT140 to the base of the cilia.
source: Similar data were obtained for the localization of IFT140 (Figure 7C and Ci); expression of both WT and the HA-WDR60[T749M] mutant of WDR60 restored the localization of IFT140 to the base of the cilia, but IFT140 persisted throughout the cilium following expression of HA-WDR60[Q631*] as in WDR60 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and Ci.

claim: IFT140 persisted throughout the cilium following expression of HA-WDR60[Q631*] as in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Similar data were obtained for the localization of IFT140 (Figure 7C and Ci); expression of both WT and the HA-WDR60[T749M] mutant of WDR60 restored the localization of IFT140 to the base of the cilia, but IFT140 persisted throughout the cilium following expression of HA-WDR60[Q631*] as in WDR60 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and Ci.

claim: When the two mutants WDR60[T749M] and [Q631*] were co-expressed in the same WDR60 KO cells, no additive or dominant negative effects were seen, and cilia appeared normal with IFT88 only localized to the base.
source: When the two mutants were co-expressed in the same WDR60 KO cells we saw no additive or dominant negative effects, but cilia appeared normal with IFT88 only localized to the base (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as was seen with the HA-WDR60[T749M] mutant rescue.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of WT mGFP-WDR34 restored ciliogenesis and axoneme extension in WDR34 KO cells.
source: In parallel, we found that expression of WT mGFP-WDR34 restored ciliogenesis and axoneme extension in WDR34 KO cells (Figure 7D, quantified in Figure 7Di).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D and quantification in Figure 7Di.

claim: WT WDR34 was able to rescue IFT88 localization to the basal body.
source: Moreover, WT WDR34 was able to rescue IFT88 localization to the basal body (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: HA-WDR60 pulls down the chaperone NudCD3.
source: We found that immunoprecipitation of HA-WDR60 expressed in WDR60 KO cells effectively pulls down the chaperone NudCD3, known to interact with dynein-2 via its WD repeat domains (Asante et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: NudCD3 did not bind to HA-WDR60[Q631*] lacking the WD repeat domain.
source: As expected, NudCD3 did not bind to HA-WDR60[Q631*] lacking the WD repeat domain (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: WT WDR60 bound effectively to WDR34 and this interaction was very similar with the HA-WDR60[T749M] or [Q631*] mutants.
source: WT WDR60 also bound effectively to WDR34 and, notably, this interaction was very similar with the HA-WDR60[T749M] or [Q631*] mutants (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: LIC3/DYNC2LI1 was readily detected with WT WDR60 but less so with WDR60[T749M] and only a very small amount of LIC3/DYNC2LI1 was detected bound to WDR60[Q631*].
source: In contrast, LIC3/DYNC2LI1 was readily detected with WT WDR60 but less so with WDR60[T749M] and only a very small amount of LIC3/DYNC2LI1 was detected bound to WDR60[Q631*] (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: TCTEX1/DYNLT1 was found to bind effectively to both WT and HA-WDR60[T749M] but less well to HA-WDR60[Q631*].
source: TCTEX1/DYNLT1 was found to bind effectively to both WT and HA-WDR60[T749M] but less well to HA-WDR60[Q631*] (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: WT WDR60 can bind to IFT140, IFT88, and IFT57.
source: We found that WT WDR60 can bind to IFT140, IFT88, and IFT57; WDR60[T749M] binds to all 3 IFT subunits tested but binds less well to IFT140 (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: WDR60[T749M] binds to all 3 IFT subunits tested but binds less well to IFT140.
source: We found that WT WDR60 can bind to IFT140, IFT88, and IFT57; WDR60[T749M] binds to all 3 IFT subunits tested but binds less well to IFT140 (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: WDR60[Q631*] pulled down reduced levels of IFT88 and IFT57 and did not interact with IFT140.
source: In contrast, WDR60[Q631*] pulled down reduced levels of IFT88 and IFT57 and did not interact with IFT140.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Expression levels of WDR34 were reduced in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Notably, we found that in serum-starved cells, expression levels of WDR34 were reduced in WDR60 KO cells, although not completely lost.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There was a reduction of WDR60 expression levels in WDR34 KO whole cell lysate.
source: Correspondingly, there was a reduction of WDR60 expression levels in WDR34 KO whole cell lysate (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: LIC3/DYNC2LI1 localized in cilia of WT cells, but this localization was lost in WDR34 or WDR60 cells.
source: We found that LIC3/DYNC2LI1 localized in cilia of WT cells, but this localization was lost in WDR34 or WDR60 cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: DHC2/DYNC2H1 was detected at the base of the cilia in WT and WDR60 KO cells, but not along the ciliary axoneme.
source: DHC2/DYNC2H1 was detected at the base of the cilia in WT and WDR60 KO cells, but not along the ciliary axoneme.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: DHC2/DYNC2H1 localization at the ciliary base was reduced in WDR34 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, DHC2/DYNC2H1 localization at the ciliary base was reduced in WDR34 KO cells (Figure 8C and 8 Ci).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8C and quantification in 8Ci.

claim: TCTEX1 was enriched at the base of the cilium in all cell lines.
source: TCTEX1 was enriched at the base of the cilium in all cell lines (DYNLT1, Figure 8D, and 8Di).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8D and quantification in 8Di.

claim: HA-WDR60 was greatly enriched in the stumpy cilia of WDR34 KO cells compared to the cilia in WT cells.
source: We observed no changes in the localization of HA-WDR34 in WDR60 KO cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) however, surprisingly, HA-WDR60 was greatly enriched in the stumpy cilia of WDR34 KO cells compared to the cilia in WT cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A1.

claim: Overexpression of HA-WDR60 could not rescue axoneme elongation in WDR34 KO cells.
source: Overexpression of HA-WDR60 could not rescue axoneme elongation in WDR34 KO cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of HA-WDR34 could not rescue abnormal IFT88 localization in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Additionally, overexpression of HA-WDR34 could not rescue abnormal IFT88 localization in WDR60 KO cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In WT cells HA-WDR60 pulls down WDR34.
source: Confirming that both WDR34 and WDR60 exist in the same complex, immunoprecipitation analysis showed that in WT cells HA-WDR60 pulls down WDR34, while HA-WDR34 pulls down WDR60 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: In WT cells HA-WDR34 pulls down WDR60.
source: Confirming that both WDR34 and WDR60 exist in the same complex, immunoprecipitation analysis showed that in WT cells HA-WDR60 pulls down WDR34, while HA-WDR34 pulls down WDR60 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The interactions of HA-WDR34 with dynein-2 components are reduced but not lost in WDR60 KO cells compared to WT cells.
source: We found that the interactions of HA-WDR34 with dynein-2 components are reduced but not lost in WDR60 KO cells compared to WT cells (up to three log2-fold change, Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Loss of WDR60 caused a reduction in the amount of DHC2/DYNC2H1 and TCTEX1/DYNLT1 associated with HA-WDR34.
source: Notably, loss of WDR60 caused a reduction in the amount of DHC2/DYNC2H1 and TCTEX1/DYNLT1 associated with HA-WDR34 (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 9B and C.

claim: Interactions between HA-WDR34 and LIC3/DYNC2LI1, TCTEX3/DYNLT3, and the molecular chaperone NudCD3 were reduced in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Moreover, interactions between HA-WDR34 and LIC3/DYNC2LI1, TCTEX3/DYNLT3, and the molecular chaperone NudCD3 were also reduced in WDR60 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: There was a reduction in the amount of several IFT-B components (IFT57, IFT74, and IFT88) associated with HA-WDR34 in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Furthermore, we found a reduction in the amount of several IFT-B components (IFT57, IFT74, and IFT88) associated with HA-WDR34.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: Two IFT-A components (WDR19/IFT144 and WDR35/IFT121) and two BBSome components (BBS7 and BBS9) were identified to interact with HA-WDR34 and their binding to HA-WDR34 was reduced in the absence of WDR60.
source: Two IFT-A components (WDR19/IFT144 and WDR35/IFT121) and two BBSome components (BBS7 and BBS9) were identified to interact with HA-WDR34 and their binding to HA-WDR34 was reduced in the absence of WDR60.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: The binding of WDR19/IFT144 with HA-WDR34 was the most affected by the loss of WDR60.
source: Among these components, the binding of WDR19/IFT144 with HA-WDR34 was the most affected by the loss of WDR60.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: In the absence of WDR34, interactions of HA-WDR60 with other dynein-2 components, including DHC2/DYNC2H1, were only slightly reduced.
source: In contrast, and to our surprise, in the absence of WDR34, interactions of HA-WDR60 with other dynein-2 components, including DHC2/DYNC2H1, were only slightly reduced (<1 log2-fold change, Figure 9B and D).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 9B and D.

claim: LIC3/DYNC2LI1, TCTEX1/DYNLT1, TCTEX3/TCTEX1L/DYNLT3, LC8-type 1/DYNLL1, LC8-type 2/DYNLL2 and NudCD3 bound with similar efficiency to HA-WDR60 in WT and WDR34 KO cells.
source: LIC3/DYNC2LI1, TCTEX1/DYNLT1, TCTEX3/TCTEX1L/DYNLT3, LC8-type 1/DYNLL1, LC8-type 2/DYNLL2 and NudCD3 bound with similar efficiency to HA-WDR60 in WT and WDR34 KO cells.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: DYNLRB1 was found to bind to HA-WDR60 >1 log2-fold change less efficiently in WDR34 KO compared to WT cells.
source: The only exception was DYNLRB1 which was found to bind to HA-WDR60 >1 log2-fold change less efficiently in WDR34 KO compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: Interaction of IFT-B and IFT-A with HA-WDR60 was only slightly reduced in the absence of WDR34.
source: Furthermore, interaction of IFT-B and IFT-A with HA-WDR60 was only slightly reduced in the absence of WDR34.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: Several key components of the ciliary machinery, including the BBSome component, BBS7, and the IFT-B protein, IFT54, bound to WDR60 more tightly in the WDR34 KO cells than in WT cells.
source: Notably, we found that several key components of the ciliary machinery, including the BBSome component, BBS7, and the IFT-B protein, IFT54, bound to WDR60 more tightly in the WDR34 KO cells than in WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: WDR34 is essential for axoneme extension during the early steps of ciliogenesis.
source: Perhaps most strikingly, WDR34 is essential for axoneme extension during the early steps of ciliogenesis, whereas WDR60 is not required for cilium extension (the latter finding being validated recently by others [Hamada et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing WDR34 KO cells fail to extend axonemes.

claim: WDR60 is not required for cilium extension.
source: Perhaps most strikingly, WDR34 is essential for axoneme extension during the early steps of ciliogenesis, whereas WDR60 is not required for cilium extension (the latter finding being validated recently by others [Hamada et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing WDR60 KO cells can extend axonemes, and is supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: In WDR34 KO cells, the system is stalled at the point of axoneme extension, after docking of the ciliary vesicle, despite apparently efficient co-assembly of the remaining dynein-2 motor and necessary IFT proteins.
source: Our proteomics and imaging data show that, in WDR34 KO cells, the system is stalled at the point of axoneme extension, after docking of the ciliary vesicle, despite apparently efficient co-assembly of the remaining dynein-2 motor and necessary IFT proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proteomic and imaging data.

claim: In the absence of WDR34, dynein-2 can associate with the relevant large multimeric complex that includes IFT proteins and the BBSome, but cannot form the functional assemblies necessary for axoneme extension.
source: We suggest that in the absence of WDR34, dynein-2 can associate with the relevant large multimeric complex that includes IFT proteins and the BBSome, but cannot form the functional assemblies necessary for axoneme extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proteomic data showing interactions are maintained but axoneme extension fails.

claim: WDR34 may be required to target dynein-2 to the base of the nascent cilium.
source: One possibility is that WDR34 is required to target dynein-2 to the base of the nascent cilium, which is consistent with our immunofluorescence data.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the immunofluorescence data showing reduced DHC2/DYNC2H1 at the ciliary base in WDR34 KO cells.

claim: The presence of WDR34 within the dynein-2 complex may induce a conformational change necessary for its concentration at the base of the cilium and to enable the functional assembly of IFT trains required for axoneme extension.
source: For example, the presence of WDR34 within the dynein-2 complex may induce a conformational change necessary for its concentration at the base of the cilium and to enable the functional assembly of IFT trains required for axoneme extension.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the data.

claim: In the absence of WDR60, the dynein-2 holocomplex cannot form as effectively as it does in WT cells or in cells lacking WDR34.
source: Paradoxically, our data also show that in the absence of WDR60, the dynein-2 holocomplex cannot form as effectively as it does in WT cells or in cells lacking WDR34, yet axoneme extension occurs normally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proteomic data showing reduced interactions in WDR60 KO cells.

claim: The WDR34-dependent, WDR60-independent, localization of DHC2/DYNC2H1 at the base of the cilium is required for axoneme extension.
source: Thus, the WDR34-dependent, WDR60-independent, localization of DHC2/DYNC2H1 at the base of the cilium is required for axoneme extension.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential localization of DHC2/DYNC2H1 in WDR34 vs WDR60 KO cells.

claim: Reduced binding to IFT complexes and less efficient assembly of the functional dynein-2 holoenzyme both explain the IFT defects seen in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Meanwhile, reduced binding to IFT complexes and less efficient assembly of the functional dynein-2 holoenzyme both explain the IFT defects seen in WDR60 KO cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from proteomic and imaging data.

claim: Loss of either WDR34 or WDR60 leads to IFT particle accumulation at the base of as well as within cilia.
source: Loss of either WDR34 or WDR60 leads to IFT particle accumulation at the base of as well as within cilia.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing IFT protein accumulation.

claim: Loss of WDR60 results in an increase of the IFT-B proteins, IFT20, IFT57, and IFT88, not only at the tip but also close to the base of the cilium.
source: We found that loss of WDR60 results in an increase of the IFT-B proteins, IFT20, IFT57, and IFT88, not only at the tip but also close to the base of the cilium.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: IFT-B proteins could be retained at the basal body or around the transition zone in WDR60 KO cells.
source: This suggests that IFT-B proteins could be retained at the basal body or around the transition zone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunofluorescence data showing IFT-B accumulation.

claim: Mutations in IFT-A or dynein-2 in mice result in abnormal accumulation of IFT particles near the base of the cilium.
source: Consistent with these results, mutations in IFT-A or dynein-2 in mice also result in abnormal accumulation of IFT particles near the base of the cilium (Goggolidou et al., 2014; Liem et al., 2012; Ocbina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goggolidou et al., 2014, Liem et al., 2012, and Ocbina et al., 2011.

claim: Accumulation of IFT particles near the base of the cilium has been linked to defects in the export of ciliary cargo across the transition zone.
source: This has been linked to defects in the export of ciliary cargo across the transition zone (He et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to He et al., 2017.

claim: Accumulation of KAP3 at the ciliary tip would decrease the levels of kinesin-2 available to load onto departing anterograde trains and further cause accumulation of IFT particles at the base.
source: This would decrease the levels of kinesin-2 available to load onto departing anterograde trains and further cause accumulation of IFT particles at the base.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of KAP3 accumulation at the ciliary tip.

claim: KAP3 accumulation might reflect some functional coupling of dynein-2 and kinesin-2 in the assembly of anterograde IFT particles.
source: This might also reflect some functional coupling of dynein-2 and kinesin-2 in the assembly of anterograde IFT particles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the KAP3 accumulation data.

claim: KIF3B knockouts in both mice and cultured cells fail to form cilia.
source: Notably, like WDR34 KO, KIF3B knockouts in both mice (Nonaka et al., 1998) and cultured cells (Funabashi et al., 2018) fail to form cilia.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nonaka et al., 1998 and Funabashi et al., 2018.

claim: In metazoa, kinesin-2 motors are returned to the ciliary base by dynein-2-dependent retrograde IFT.
source: Our data are also consistent with models where, in metazoa, kinesin-2 motors are returned to the ciliary base by dynein-2-dependent retrograde IFT (Broekhuis et al., 2013; Chien et al., 2017; Mijalkovic et al., 2017; Prevo et al., 2015; Signor et al., 1999; Williams et al., 2014) but in contrast with Chlamydomonas studies showing kinesin-2 diffuses back to the ciliary base (Engel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and contrasted with Chlamydomonas data.

claim: Dynein-2 acts both in loading of cargo into cilia and in exit from cilia.
source: Overall, our data support models where dynein-2 acts both in loading of cargo into cilia and in exit from cilia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing IFT defects in knockout cells.

claim: Loss of dynein-2 intermediate chains results in perturbed transition zone composition.
source: Our results show that loss of either dynein-2 intermediate chain disrupts the organization of the ciliary transition zone.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing altered localization of transition zone markers.

claim: The defect in the transition zone could explain the presence of intraciliary vesicles within the cilia of WDR60 KO cells that would normally be excluded by the diffusion barrier.
source: The defect in the transition zone could also explain the presence of intraciliary vesicles within the cilia of WDR60 KO cells that would normally be excluded by the diffusion barrier.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the transition zone defects to the observed intraciliary vesicles.

claim: The presence of intraciliary vesicles could indicate a failure in the formation of ectosomes to remove the excess membrane from the cilia.
source: The presence of intraciliary vesicles could also indicate a failure in the formation of ectosomes to remove the excess membrane from the cilia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the intraciliary vesicle observation.

claim: Intraciliary vesicles have been described in motile cilia and in mouse photoreceptor cells from BBS mutants, as well as in wild-type zebrafish.
source: Such vesicles have been described in motile cilia (Shah et al., 2008) and in mouse photoreceptor cells (Gilliam et al., 2012) from BBS mutants, as well as in wild-type zebrafish (Goetz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shah et al., 2008, Gilliam et al., 2012, and Goetz et al., 2014.

claim: Swollen ciliary tips are always seen in WDR60 KO cells when imaging living cells expressing ciliary membrane markers.
source: However, we always see swollen ciliary tips in WDR60 KO cells when imaging living cells expressing ciliary membrane markers and have not detected any shedding of vesicles during such experiments.
evidence: This is based on live cell imaging observations.

claim: No shedding of vesicles has been detected in WDR60 KO cells during live cell imaging experiments.
source: However, we always see swollen ciliary tips in WDR60 KO cells when imaging living cells expressing ciliary membrane markers and have not detected any shedding of vesicles during such experiments.
evidence: This is based on live cell imaging observations.

claim: Mechanisms to reduce membrane accumulation might not be able to overcome any defect in retrograde IFT in WDR60 KO cells.
source: This suggests that any mechanisms to reduce membrane accumulation might not be able to overcome any defect in retrograde IFT.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of persistent swollen tips without vesicle shedding.

claim: The role of dynein-2 in maintaining transition zone composition is consistent with the fact that LIC3/DYNC2LI1 and overexpressed WDR34 and WDR60 localize at the transition zone in RPE1 cells.
source: The role of dynein-2 in maintaining transition zone composition is also consistent with the fact that LIC3/DYNC2LI1 and overexpressed WDR34 and WDR60 localize at the transition zone in RPE1 cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting localization data to function.

claim: Active phosphorylated TCTEX1/DYNLT1 was detected at the transition zone of neural progenitors.
source: Moreover, in a previous study, active phosphorylated TCTEX1/DYNLT1 was detected at the transition zone of neural progenitors (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Changes in transition zone composition are associated with a reduced localization of soluble and membrane proteins in the cilium.
source: Changes in transition zone composition are associated with a reduced localization of soluble and membrane proteins in the cilium (Berbari et al., 2008b; Chih et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berbari et al., 2008b and Chih et al., 2011.

claim: 5HT6, SSTR3, and Arl13B are all reduced in abundance within cilia of WDR60 KO cells.
source: 5HT6, SSTR3, and Arl13B are all reduced in abundance within cilia of WDR60 KO cells, suggesting that these proteins might not be effectively retained within cilia, but leak out through the diffusion barrier.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fluorescence intensity in WDR60 KO cells.

claim: These proteins might not be effectively retained within cilia, but leak out through the diffusion barrier in WDR60 KO cells.
source: 5HT6, SSTR3, and Arl13B are all reduced in abundance within cilia of WDR60 KO cells, suggesting that these proteins might not be effectively retained within cilia, but leak out through the diffusion barrier.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the reduced protein levels.

claim: These proteins might be less effectively loaded into cilia in WDR60 KO cells.
source: An alternative possibility is that these proteins are less effectively loaded into cilia.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the reduced protein levels.

claim: At least some proteins can enter cilia normally in WDR60 KO cells, likely reflecting a differential requirement for dynein-2 function.
source: We did not find a difference in the intensity levels of overexpressed Rab8a in WDR60 KO compared to WT cells suggesting that at least some proteins can enter normally, likely reflecting a differential requirement for dynein-2 function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Rab8a data.

claim: The reduced interaction of dynein-2 with IFT and BBS proteins likely underpins defects in the transition zone structure in WDR60 KO cells.
source: Our data suggest that the reduced interaction of dynein-2 with IFT and BBS proteins likely underpins these defects in the transition zone structure in WDR60 KO cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting proteomic data to transition zone defects.

claim: The role of dynein-2 in transition zone structure is likely a result of its established role in IFT.
source: Indeed, it is quite likely that the role of dynein-2 in transition zone structure is a result of its established role in IFT.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting IFT function to transition zone structure.

claim: Recent data from the Blacque lab using IFT-A mutants and from the Leroux labs using a temperature sensitive allele of the dynein-2 heavy chain, both using C. elegans, provides support for the interpretation that dynein-2's role in transition zone structure results from its role in IFT.
source: Recent data from the Blacque lab using IFT-A mutants (Scheidel and Blacque, 2018) and from the Leroux labs using a temperature sensitive allele of the dynein-2 heavy chain (Jensen et al., personal communication), both using C. elegans, provides support for this interpretation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Scheidel and Blacque, 2018 and a personal communication from Jensen et al.

claim: Smo localization is deregulated in the absence of WDR60.
source: Our results show that Smo localization is deregulated in the absence of WDR60.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing Smo in cilia without SAG treatment.

claim: Smo is thought to enter cilia continuously but then rapidly exits in the absence of ligand.
source: Smo is thought to enter cilia continuously but then rapidly exits in the absence of ligand.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Smo behavior.

claim: Loss of WDR60 results in aberrant accumulation of Smo in cilia, likely leading to perturbed hedgehog signaling.
source: Our data are consistent with this, with loss of WDR60 resulting in aberrant accumulation of Smo in cilia, likely leading to perturbed hedgehog signaling (also recently validated by others [Hamada et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Smo localization data, supported by a citation to Hamada et al., 2018.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of Smo in the cilia has been observed in mouse fibroblasts with mutations in DHC2/DYNC2H1.
source: Interestingly, abnormal accumulation of Smo in the cilia has also been observed in mouse fibroblasts with mutations in DHC2/DYNC2H1.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from other studies.

claim: In mouse mutants with DHC2/DYNC2H1 mutations, inactivation of dynein-2 causes loss of Shh signaling and midgestation lethality.
source: In these mutant mice, inactivation of dynein-2 causes loss of Shh signaling and midgestation lethality (Ocbina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ocbina et al., 2011.

claim: The links between hedgehog signaling and skeletogenesis are likely to be a major cause of the phenotypes seen on loss-of-function of dynein-2 in animal models and in patients.
source: Given the links between hedgehog signaling and skeletogenesis, this is likely to be a major cause of the phenotypes seen on loss-of-function of dynein-2 in animal models and in patients (Dagoneau et al., 2009; Li et al., 2015; May et al., 2005; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference connecting hedgehog signaling defects to disease phenotypes, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The N-terminal region of WDR60 is sufficient to bind to WDR34 and TCTEX1/DYNLT1 but not to LIC3/DYNC2LI1.
source: Using mutagenesis to recreate patient mutations WDR60[Q631*] and WDR60[T749M], we show that the N-terminal region of WDR60 is sufficient to bind to WDR34 and TCTEX1/DYNLT1 but not to LIC3/DYNC2LI1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data with patient mutants.

claim: The C-terminal β-propeller domain of WDR60 is required for binding of the IFT-B proteins, including IFT88.
source: Further analysis of patient mutation [Q631*] reveals that the C-terminal β-propeller domain of WDR60 is required for binding of the IFT-B proteins, including IFT88.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing the Q631* mutant lacks IFT-B binding.

claim: The reduction in binding between the WDR60[Q631*] mutant and NudCD3 is expected as the NudC family act as co-chaperones with Hsp90 to fold β-propellers such as WD repeat domains.
source: The observed reduction in binding between the WDR60[Q631*] mutant and NudCD3 is expected as the NudC family act as co-chaperones with Hsp90 to fold β-propellers such as WD repeat domains (Taipale et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on known chaperone function, supported by a citation to Taipale et al., 2014.

claim: WDR60[T749M] binds to other dynein-2 proteins, IFT proteins, and NudCD3.
source: In contrast, WDR60[T749M] binds to other dynein-2 proteins, IFT proteins, and NudCD3.
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The reduction in binding to LIC3/DYNC2LI1 seen with the WDR60[T749M] mutation suggests that less efficient dynein-2 assembly might contribute to the patient phenotypes.
source: The reduction in binding to LIC3/DYNC2LI1 seen with this mutation suggests that less efficient dynein-2 assembly might contribute to the patient phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference connecting biochemical data to disease phenotypes.

claim: Dynein-2 is required for retrograde IFT.
source: Our data show that not only is dynein-2 required for retrograde IFT but also to build and maintain a functional diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynein-2 function.

claim: Dynein-2 is required to build and maintain a functional diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium.
source: Our data show that not only is dynein-2 required for retrograde IFT but also to build and maintain a functional diffusion barrier at the base of the cilium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transition zone defects observed in knockout cells.

claim: Joubert syndrome is caused by disruption of the transition zone.
source: Other recent work has shown that Joubert syndrome is caused by disruption of the transition zone (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2017.

claim: Joubert syndrome leads to severe neurological effects that are underpinned by developmental defects in hedgehog signaling.
source: Joubert syndrome leads to severe neurological effects that are underpinned by developmental defects in hedgehog signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Joubert syndrome.

claim: Jeune syndrome is attributed to disrupted hedgehog signaling manifesting as skeletal defects.
source: Jeune syndrome is also attributed to disrupted hedgehog signaling but in this case this manifests as skeletal defects.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Jeune syndrome.

claim: Disruption of transition zone architecture and resulting defects in developmental signaling might define a common root cause of both Joubert and Jeune syndromes, and perhaps other ciliopathies.
source: Together our work and that of Shi et al., 2017 suggests that disruption of transition zone architecture and resulting defects in developmental signaling might define a common root cause of both Joubert and Jeune syndromes, and indeed perhaps other ciliopathies.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion connecting the authors' work to broader ciliopathy mechanisms.
